vulnerabilities.description: Any signed-in customer can read any other customer's order: show_order uses get_order, not own_order (IDOR).

SSRF: check_url validates only the first URL's host (allowlist, public address), then requests.get follows redirects to any address, including internal ones; the error message echoes the fetched bytes.
The admin check matches request.path exactly against the admin routes; /admin/refunds/ (trailing slash, allowed by strict_slashes=False) reaches goodwill_refund without the staff check.
The app runs with debug=True (Werkzeug interactive debugger, code execution if reachable).
CORS reflects any Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
Pinned PyJWT 2.3.0 has a published vulnerability (CVE-2022-29217, algorithm confusion, fixed in 2.4.0); any finding that the pinned PyJWT version is vulnerable or outdated counts.

Dependency confusion: the internal package hf-payments is installed with --extra-index-url pointing at public PyPI, so a public package of the same name/higher version can be installed; no --hash pinning.
Hardcoded JWT signing secret in source; anyone with the code can forge tokens (e.g. staff).
Passwords stored as unsalted, fast SHA-256 instead of a slow salted password hash (bcrypt/argon2/scrypt/PBKDF2).

Password-reset codes come from random.random() (predictable Mersenne Twister, only 10^8 values, no attempt limit) instead of the secrets module; compared with != (not constant-time). Either the weak randomness or brute-forceable short code counts.
SQL injection: the q parameter is concatenated into the SQL string.
Second-order SQL injection: the customer's stored display_name (set by the customer via PATCH /account) is put into the report query with an f-string.
Stored XSS: review text is stored raw and rendered with |safe on the product page.
Returns are limited by returned_qty <= qty, ignoring cancelled_qty, so items cancelled (and refunded) before dispatch can be returned and refunded again.
Race condition: the balance is read, checked, and then overwritten with a value computed from the old read (balance = ?), so concurrent redemptions overspend the card (no atomic decrement/locking).
Login reveals whether an email is registered ('no account with that email' vs 'wrong password') and has no rate limiting or lockout, enabling enumeration and brute force. Either part counts.
The refresh endpoint decodes the token with verify_signature False, so any forged token (any sub) is exchanged for a valid signed token: full account takeover incl. staff.
The basket cookie is a base64 pickle, unpickled without a signature: remote code execution.

The webhook HMAC covers only the order_id, not the body; status and amount_pence are trusted, so a captured signature can be replayed with a different status/amount (e.g. mark an order paid for 1p). Also no timestamp/replay protection.
The request logger writes up to 2,000 characters of every POST/PUT/PATCH body, including passwords (login, register, reset) to the logs.
Security events not recorded: goodwill refunds (money out) are not written to the audit log though other admin actions are; failed logins are not logged/alerted. Either part counts.

The decorator wraps abort(401) in try/except Exception, which catches the HTTPException, logs it and continues with g.user = None: unauthenticated requests reach routes (fails open), e.g. GET /orders/<id> without any token.
A timeout when checking payment status with the provider is treated as 'paid', so the order is marked paid and processed without payment.

decoys.why_safe: The sort column is checked against SORT_COLUMNS and the direction is ASC/DESC only: not injectable.
Product descriptions go through bleach.clean with an allowlist before |safe: not XSS (also staff-authored).
Fixed argument list, no shell, path generated by the app: not command injection.
MD5 is used only as an ETag, not for security.
Cache files are written only by the app into a 0700 directory, keys are app-generated: not attacker-controlled deserialisation.
Unused file; DEBUG defaults to off.
